title: Judging a historian's argument

draft.title: Judging a historian's argument
card: A historian's interpretation is an argument about the past. It is built from evidence, and it can be judged.
Ask what evidence the historian uses and whether it is enough. Also ask what the historian leaves out, since missing voices or sources can weaken an argument.
Ask when the work was written. Historians can use only the sources and ideas available to them then, and new evidence may later change the picture.
Ask what questions or values shaped the work. A historian's interests influence what they look for, so two historians can reach different views from the same period.
draft.remember: Judge an argument by its evidence, its gaps, its date and the values behind it.

a.q: A historian's book on a 1950s migrant camp uses only government files. Which is the fairest criticism?
opts: It leaves out the voices of the migrants themselves
It is weak, because government files are never evidence
It must be wrong, because it is about the 1950s
It is biased, because it uses written sources
a.why: Using only government files leaves out what residents experienced, which is a gap worth noting. Government files are still evidence, so the claim that they are not is wrong.

b.q: A 1960s history of a colonial frontier ignores Aboriginal accounts. A 2010s historian disagrees using oral histories. Which is the best judgement?
opts: The 1960s work reflects its time and left out sources
The 2010s work is right, because it is newer
The 1960s work is right, because it is older
The two works cannot be compared at all
b.why: The date and the questions of the time shaped what the earlier historian sought, and the omission of Aboriginal accounts weakens the argument. Newer does not automatically mean right: the 2010s work must also be judged by its evidence.
b.clue: Consider both the date and what was left out.

a.best: It leaves out the voices of the migrants themselves

b.best: The 1960s work reflects its time and left out sources

problems.detail: Two distractors use absolutes ('must be wrong', 'never evidence'), so a student can rule them out without knowing the idea. Only one distractor ('biased, because it uses written sources') needs real thought.
The clue 'Ask whose view is missing' points straight to the only option about missing voices, which gives the answer away.
The clue 'Consider both the date and what was left out' matches the right option's wording ('reflects its time and left out sources') almost word for word, which gives the answer away.

check.summary: The card and both answers are accurate. Both clues nearly name the right option, and question a's absolute distractors are too easy to rule out. Question b involves Aboriginal accounts of colonial frontier history, so it is flagged for review.

proposal.title: Judging a historian's argument
card: A historian's interpretation is an argument about the past. Historians rarely saw the events themselves, so they build their case from evidence, and it can be judged.
Ask what evidence the historian uses and whether it is enough. Any kind of source, written or spoken, can be evidence, but missing voices or sources can weaken an argument.
Ask when the work was written, not just when the events happened. Historians can use only the sources and ideas available to them then, and new evidence may later change the picture.
Ask what questions or values shaped the work. A historian's interests influence what they look for, so two historians can reach different views from the same period.
proposal.remember: Judge an argument by its evidence, its gaps, its date and the values behind it.

a.q: A historian's book on a 1950s migrant camp uses only government files. Which is the fairest criticism?
opts: It leaves out the migrants' own accounts of camp life
It is unreliable, because the historian did not see the camp
It is out of date, because it is about events in the 1950s
It is biased, because it relies on written records
a.why: Using only government files leaves out what the migrants experienced, which is a gap that can weaken the argument. Written records are still evidence, and historians rarely see the events they study, so those are not fair criticisms.
a.clue: Is the evidence enough to cover the whole topic?

b.q: A 1960s history of a colonial frontier ignores Aboriginal accounts. A 2010s historian disagrees using oral histories. Which is the best judgement?
opts: The 1960s work is weakened by the accounts it left out
The 2010s work is more reliable because it is newer
The 1960s work is more reliable because it is older
Works written 50 years apart cannot be fairly compared
b.why: The questions of the 1960s shaped what the earlier historian looked for, and leaving out Aboriginal accounts weakens the argument. Being newer does not make a work right on its own: the 2010s work must also be judged by its evidence.
b.clue: Look at the sources each historian chose to use.
